cases.question: What is the unmet flight demand in SFO airport and why?

runs.answer:
SFO scores 64.4 on the unmet-demand lens (0-100). The score is inferred from proxies, because no source observes unmet demand directly. The main driver is a high load factor. Delays add to it, and growth pulls it down slightly.
- Load factor: 0.8231 (82.31%) of seats filled in 2025, which is the 86.5th percentile. This raises the score the most.
- Delay: 60.9th percentile. 18.93% of 143,415 domestic departures in 2025 were delayed 15+ minutes. Excess taxi-out of 8.4305 minutes is at the 84.8th percentile.
- Growth: 45.8th percentile, which lowers the score. The FAA forecasts enplanement growth of 3.13% a year to 2034 (86th percentile). Actual growth since FY2019 was -2.18% a year (5.6th percentile).
- Utilization context: operations were 94.76% of capacity in 2024 (90.8th percentile). Capacity is 402,400 operations per year, an FAA profile figure that the tool labels measured.

cases.question: Which data system do you use for delays?

runs.answer: Delays come from the BTS Airline On-Time Performance dataset (the "ontime" source). It covers domestic reporting carriers only and includes delays and taxi-out. For the score, the snapshot runs from 202301 to 202512. Live ground stops and delay programs are a separate source, the FAA NAS status feed. That feed is not part of the score.

Delays in the Capacity Pressure Score come from the BTS Airline On-Time Performance dataset (ontime), which covers domestic reporting carriers. It also supplies taxi-out data and spans 202301 to 202512. Live conditions such as ground stops, ground delay programs and closures come from the separate FAA NAS status feed. That feed is not part of the frozen score.

cases.question: What rules decide whether a flight counts as long haul?

runs.answer: A flight counts as long haul when its segment is 3,000 miles or more. The long-haul share is long-haul departures divided by all departures. It comes from BTS T-100 segment data, which covers all carriers, cargo flights included. For JFK in 2025, the tool reports 52,786 long-haul departures out of 220,185 total, a share of 0.2397 (23.97%). That puts JFK at the 99.3rd percentile of hub airports. Long haul carries 10% of the Capacity Pressure Score weight. The tools don't give any further rules, such as how distance is measured or how segments are classified.

A flight counts as long haul when its segment distance is 3,000 miles or more. The long-haul share is that kind of departure as a share of an airport's departures in a year. The distance and departure counts come from the BTS T-100 Segment data, which covers all carriers. Long haul carries a 10% weight in the Capacity Pressure Score. It is also the basis of the long_haul ranking lens. I can show an airport's long-haul share, with its year and departure count, if you name one.

cases.question: Can an analyst override the weights, or are they fixed in the config?

runs.answer: I can't confirm whether an analyst can override the weights. None of my tools expose a setting for that, and nothing I can see says whether they sit in a config file. What I can say is that every score I return uses one fixed set of weights, scoring version 1.1.0: utilization 0.3 (30%), delay 0.25 (25%), growth 0.2 (20%), load factor 0.15 (15%) and long haul 0.1 (10%). None of my tools accept a weight parameter, so I can't re-run a ranking with different weights. The lens options (expansion, congestion, unmet_demand, long_haul) change which score I use as the headline, not the weights. To find out whether the weights can be changed, ask whoever maintains the scoring config.
